summary: CIPR plants data-exfiltration payloads (direct, or an indirect call to a hidden script) into 20 real repos (5 each in Python, JS, C, Java). It then varies what the benign user asks: 4 tasks (prepare environment, run tests, fix bug, implement feature), 4 prompt styles (baseline plus 3 styles clustered from social-media prompts) and 3 skill/rule settings (none, GitHub productivity skills, skills plus security rules). 1,920 Docker runs on Codex + GPT-5.4 measure attack success via a mock HTTP server and alerts via a human-validated GPT-4o judge, with smaller runs on Codex + GPT-5.5, OpenCode and Claude Code. Task type dominates: Run-Tests gives 45.5% attack success with 9.4% alerts. Security rules raise alerts but do not lower attack success. Prompt-style effects are small and marginal.

claims.claim: Task type creates up to a 4.5-fold difference in ASR; Run-Tests is a silent attack surface (high ASR, low AR)
claims.evidence: Table 14A (N about 480 per task, Codex + GPT-5.4): Run-Tests ASR 45.5% [41.1, 50.0] vs Fix-Bug 8.6% [6.4, 11.5]. That ratio is 5.3x, not 4.5x. Run-Tests AR 9.4% vs Prepare-Env 34.9%. Conditional on the injected file being read, ASR is 51.3% vs 26.4% (Table 1). Robust Wilson CIs for the main agent.

claims.claim: Underspecified prompts reduce ASR by truncating execution depth
claims.evidence: Table 13: TIU adjusted OR 0.71 [0.51, 0.98], p=0.036; omnibus chi-square p=0.048; no correction for the three style contrasts. The three styles were picked from 15 clusters as the 'most distinctive' in a preliminary ASR run on a subset of the same benchmark (§3.2), i.e., selected on the outcome. The depth mechanism rests on one case (qmk: 52 vs 37 tool calls) with P(read) unchanged, and §4.2 states the opposite mechanism ('explores the project more thoroughly'). TIU also cuts task success (62.3% vs 54.7%).

claims.claim: Security-aware rules increase alerts but do not significantly reduce attack success
claims.evidence: Table 14C: ASR 22.6 / 25.5 / 22.3 (no skills / skills / skills plus security rules), CIs overlapping; AR 10.5 to 14.8. The discussion attributes the gap to alerts arriving after execution. Normal skills also lower task success, 64.3% to 55.8% in Table 14 but only 36.8% to 35.2% in Table 17 for the same configuration, an unexplained inconsistency.

claims.claim: Key patterns generalize across agents and models: Run-Tests has the highest ASR and lowest AR in all four configurations, and prompt-style ordering is stable
claims.evidence: Table 15: lowest AR is Fix-Bug or Fix-Feature in every configuration, not Run-Tests. OpenCode Run-Tests vs Prepare-Env ASR is 13.1 vs 12.2 (overlapping). Claude Code + Sonnet 4.6 stays at 12.2% or below on every task. Table 16: style ordering changes between agents, and all style CIs overlap within each agent.

claims.claim: The LLM alert oracle is reliable
claims.evidence: App. G.1: 192 traces, two annotators (kappa 0.86), LLM vs adjudicated consensus kappa 0.83, F1 0.85; aggregate AR identical (10.42%).

patterns.note: Instruction-level defence (security directives added to skills/rules) vs none, same 1,920-run design: ASR unchanged (22.6% vs 22.3%) though alerts rise to 14.8%. Alerts often fire after the payload has run. Only text-level defences are tested; the authors recommend control-flow blocking instead.
Rules supplied as agent instructions change behaviour (more alerts) but not outcomes (no ASR drop). Consistent with instruction files being advisory, not enforcement.

Generic productivity skills scraped from GitHub vs no skills: task success drops (64.3% to 55.8%, non-overlapping CIs in Table 14) and ASR rises slightly (22.6% to 25.5%). Table 17 shows a much smaller TSR drop for the same runs. These are generic, not task-tailored skills.
Recommends deterministic blocking when an alert fires and hierarchical pre-execution review of config and test files. Not implemented or tested.
Docker isolation with a mock exfiltration server is the evaluation substrate; implies egress control is the real mitigation but does not test it.
Only unconstrained automation mode was tested; approval and human-in-the-loop modes are explicitly out of scope.
Prepare-Env and Run-Tests on an unfamiliar third-party repo is the first step of exploring or onboarding to a codebase, and these are the highest-ASR invocations measured.

Underspecified (TIU) prompts lower task success and ASR because the agent 'simply does less'. Whether agents ask for clarification is not measured. The suggested rewrite of user prompts into a canonical well-specified form is untested.
GPT-4o alert judge validated against adjudicated human labels (kappa 0.83), a reasonable validation pattern for trace-based oracles.

methodology.sample: Main: 1,920 runs (20 repos x 4 tasks x 4 prompt styles x 3 skill settings x 2 payload methods), 1,917 evaluable. Cross-agent: about 640 runs per configuration (some skill settings partial).
methodology.baselines: Baseline prompt style; no skills/rules; Prepare-Env as reference task
methodology.models: Codex + GPT-5.4 (main); Codex + GPT-5.5; OpenCode + GPT-5.4; Claude Code + Claude Sonnet 4.6; GPT-4o as alert judge
methodology.variance: One run per instance (no repeated seeds, acknowledged). Wilson 95% CIs, chi-square omnibus, logistic regression with HC1 errors. No multiple-comparison correction.
methodology.ablations: Full factorial over task, style and skills; direct vs indirect payload as replicate
methodology.contamination_controls: n/a (security benchmark); payload is a documented curl exfiltration
methodology.languages: Python, JavaScript, C, Java (5 repos each, e.g., RxJava, mybatis-plus)

standards.artifacts: Dataset, payloads and execution code on GitHub (StarConnor/CIPR); style descriptions released, original social-media screenshots not

biases.detail: The three prompt styles were chosen from 15 clusters because they were the most distinctive in a preliminary ASR run on a subset of the same benchmark, then tested for significance on that benchmark.
Mechanism claims (execution depth, security salience) rest on one hand-picked matched case each.
The full factorial (all skill settings) runs only on Codex + GPT-5.4; other agents mainly get the no-skills setting.
No repeated runs per instance; run-to-run variance of agent behaviour is unknown.
'Profoundly influence', 'rigorously validate' and 'agent-agnostic in direction' overstate p=0.036/0.048 style effects and the cross-agent tables.
TSR for identical configurations differs between Table 14 (64.3%) and Table 17 (36.8%). The §4.2 mechanism contradicts §5.2. '4.5-fold' does not match the reported 45.5% vs 8.6%.

coi.detail: Independent academic security study; Claude Code comes out as most resistant without any author link to Anthropic.

verdict_reason: Large factorial design on real repos in four languages including Java, three agent harnesses, a human-validated oracle, binary-outcome statistics and released artifacts. The task-type and rules-don't-prevent findings are solid for the main agent. The prompt-style findings were selected on the outcome and are marginal, the cross-agent generalisation claims are contradicted by the paper's own tables, and two tables disagree on task success.
applicability: Directly relevant to how a discovery or onboarding harness should run agents in unfamiliar code. The most natural onboarding request, 'set up and run the tests', is the riskiest one measured (45% ASR, 9% alerts on Codex + GPT-5.4), and security prose in AGENTS.md or skills does not stop execution. For the team: (1) keep exploration and question-answering sessions read-only and separate from sessions that execute build or test scripts; (2) run anything that executes in a sandbox with egress denied by default, decided by qr or the host permission layer rather than by rules text; (3) treat build files (pom.xml or Gradle plugins, test setup) from third-party, vendored or newly cloned repos as untrusted input; (4) set per-host policy, since vulnerability differs about 4x between hosts (Claude Code vs Codex on Run-Tests). Internal repos are lower-risk than deliberately poisoned public ones, but upstream dependencies and contributor-account compromise are the stated threat paths.

conflicts_with.detail: AgentGuard finds conditional, routed instruction-level guardrails cut abnormal executions from 69.0% to 26.7%. Here generic security directives raise alerts without lowering attack success. The difference may be targeted vs generic rules, and an adversarial step vs a planted script.
pikit reports prompt-level defences lowering pooled ASR from 6.00% to 1.69% on a pre-selected subset. Here security rules leave ASR unchanged (22.6% vs 22.3%).
